summary:
HabitatPulse is an offline-first crew health and habitat monitoring prototype for long-duration space missions. It combines crew check-ins with habitat data, including carbon dioxide, temperature, and relative humidity, in one workspace.
Crew members can record wellbeing, sleep, hydration, vital signs, and symptoms. Database-backed trend charts help crew and medical reviewers identify changes over time. A statistical anomaly-screening layer flags unusual environmental readings, while a transparent rule engine identifies possible health patterns, such as low wellbeing with headache or sleep and fatigue concerns.
HabitatPulse provides explainable evidence, uncertainty statements, printable reports, and an offline Ground Medical handover queue. This supports timely human review and communication when a live connection is unavailable. The system is a prototype only and does not diagnose illness, prescribe medication, or replace qualified medical professionals.
details:
HabitatPulse is a health and habitat monitoring website for astronauts and space workers on long space missions. Our main focus is to help users understand possible links between crew health and habitat conditions. In a spacecraft or space habitat, crew members live in a closed environment for a long time. Changes in carbon dioxide (CO₂), temperature, or humidity may affect comfort, sleep, tiredness, concentration, and general wellbeing. When a crew member reports symptoms such as headache, fatigue, poor sleep, or low wellbeing, it is useful to also check what was happening in the habitat at that time.

A crew member can sign in and complete a daily check-in. The check-in form records wellbeing, mood and stress, sleep hours, sleep quality, water intake, energy level, activity level, appetite, vital signs, symptoms, and safety answers. Vital signs can include heart rate, blood oxygen, breathing rate, body temperature, weight, and heart-rate variability. The information is stored in a local MySQL database so that it can be viewed later as health trends.

The Overview page gives a quick health summary. It shows the latest check-in, latest wellbeing score, total records, and crew wellbeing graphs. These graphs help users compare changes in sleep, water intake, mood, and wellbeing over time. The Environment page shows CO₂, temperature, and relative humidity records. Users can select different time ranges and view the data in clear charts. Health and environment trends can be viewed together so crew members and medical reviewers can look for possible links over time.

For environment data, we use a local machine learning anomaly-screening model. The model checks past sensor readings and gives an anomaly score when a reading looks unusual compared with normal patterns in the data. It can flag unusual CO₂, temperature, or humidity readings. Nearby flagged readings are grouped into a persistent event, so a reviewer can see whether it may be a continuing pattern instead of only one unusual point. The model is only used to highlight data for human review. It does not prove that a habitat condition caused a health problem, and it does not make a safety decision by itself.

For health data, we made a Python rule engine. The rule engine uses clear “if” rules instead of hidden decisions. For example, it can show a possible review pattern when low wellbeing appears with headache, or when low sleep appears with fatigue. It checks the entered answers, symptoms, and available environment context. It then creates an evidence card that explains why a pattern was shown, what information supports it, and what information may be missing. This makes the result easier for crew members and medical reviewers to understand.

The Evidence page combines health check-ins, rule-engine results, and habitat context. It also shows uncertainty statements because missing data or one pattern alone should not be treated as a diagnosis. The Reports page creates a printable report with charts, evidence, and crew notes. A report can also be saved in a local Ground Medical handover queue. On the Ground Medical page, a reviewer can open a queued report, read the evidence, view health and environment trends, select a review status, and save a local reply.

We used React, TypeScript, Vite, CSS, Python, MySQL, JSON, and a saved local machine learning model. We used GitHub to share our code. Our demo records are clearly marked as simulated or historical replay data.

Our idea is creative because it connects astronaut self-check-ins, habitat sensor data, machine learning screening, explainable rule-based review, reports, and a local handover workflow in one simple system. We considered limited connection, clear graphs, simple language, human medical review, and the need to avoid false medical claims. HabitatPulse is a prototype only. It does not diagnose illness, prescribe medicine, or replace qualified medical professionals.
